Consult Summary:
- Young adult with known asthma presenting with 2–3 days of exertional shortness of breath, wheeze and cough; working impression is an acute asthma exacerbation (consider viral trigger and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction as contributors); plan: increase inhaled steroid temporarily, use salbutamol PRN, arrange GP face-to-face review with chest exam and peak flow, and escalate to A&E if worsening.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - 2–3 days of chest tightness, wheeze, cough and increased breathlessness.
  - Symptoms first noted while running (unable to talk during run), now also provoked by brisk walking.
- Timeline / progression:
  - Symptoms began ~2–3 days ago while exercising; patient reports asthma previously well controlled until this episode.
- Exacerbating / relieving factors:
  - Exacerbated by exertion (running, brisk walking).
  - Using blue reliever (salbutamol) as needed and sometimes daily; patient reports it has not helped much.
  - Uses brown preventer (Clenil) twice daily; clinician advised temporarily increasing preventer dose while awaiting GP review.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - Wheeze and cough present.
  - No sputum production reported.
  - Has hay fever (seasonal allergic rhinitis).
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No fever reported.
  - No sputum production/green phlegm.
  - No recent oral steroid courses remembered.
  - No prior hospital admissions for asthma.
  - No medication allergies reported.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma — background diagnosis discussed; previous exacerbation ~3–4 years ago; last asthma review ~2 years ago.
- Allergic rhinitis / hay fever.
- Possible eczema (patient reports some issues consistent with eczema; topical hydrocortisone and emollient discussed).
- No history of hospital admission for asthma documented.

Medications:
- Salbutamol (blue inhaler) — current reliever; frequency: used as needed and sometimes daily; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Clenil (brown inhaler — beclometasone) — preventer; patient reports previously 3 puffs twice daily. Clinician advised increasing to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting GP.
- Topical hydrocortisone — use mentioned; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Cetraben (emollient) — use mentioned; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Note: Early in visit patient mentioned “Flanel Bactroban” then corrected to “Cetraben” — discrepancy in topical medication name (conflict noted).
- Allergies: none reported.

Social History:
- Physically active — runs regularly; symptoms began during running.
- Smoking status not documented.
- Alcohol/substance use not documented.
- Occupation not documented.

Family History:
- Brother with asthma.
- Sister with eczema.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded (clinician planned chest examination and peak flow at face-to-face GP review).

Investigations:
- Peak flow: patient reports usual baseline ≈ 380 L/min; no current peak flow value recorded.
- No laboratory tests or imaging reported or performed during this consult.

Assessment & Plan:

- Overall Impression:
  - Working diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation, likely triggered by exertion and possibly a viral respiratory illness; exercise-induced bronchoconstriction may be a contributing mechanism.

- DDx Integration (brief):
  1. Acute asthma exacerbation — High likelihood.
     - Supporting: known asthma, recent onset wheeze/cough, exertional dyspnea, increased SABA use, current symptoms despite reliever.
     - Opposing: no objective current peak flow or exam documented.
  2. Viral respiratory infection triggering asthma exacerbation — Medium likelihood.
     - Supporting: short duration cough/wheeze commonly follows viral URTI.
     - Opposing: no systemic viral symptoms (fever, myalgia) reported.
  3. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) — Medium likelihood.
     - Supporting: symptoms first noted during running and provoked by exertion; atopic history (hay fever).
     - Opposing: symptoms are persistent beyond exercise and reliever appears less effective.
  - No conflict between DDx and transcript regarding likely causes; medication name discrepancy noted above (conflict noted).

- Issue 1: Acute asthma exacerbation
  - Assessment:
    - Mild–moderate symptomatic exacerbation of asthma over 2–3 days with exertional limitation; objective severity not documented (no current peak flow or exam).
  - Plan:
    - Arrange face-to-face GP review in next few days for chest examination and current peak flow measurement.
    - Interim inhaler instructions provided:
      - Increase brown inhaler (Clenil/beclometasone) to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting GP (temporary measure per clinician).
      - Use salbutamol inhaler PRN; permitted frequency up to every 2–4 hours if symptomatic (clinician cautioned that very frequent use indicates poor control).
    - Safety netting:
      - If breathing worsens despite above measures or if patient deteriorates, go to A&E promptly rather than waiting for GP review.
    - Possible escalation after GP review:
      - Consider oral corticosteroid course and/or antibiotics if indicated based on exam/peak flow and infectious features.

- Issue 2: Possible viral respiratory infection precipitating asthma worsening
  - Assessment:
    - Viral bronchitis/URTI is a plausible trigger for this exacerbation but no systemic viral features recorded.
  - Plan:
    - Symptomatic management; GP to assess for focal chest signs, fever, sputum changes.
    - Reserve antibiotics for clinical features consistent with bacterial infection per GP assessment.

- Issue 3: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (contributor)
  - Assessment:
    - EIB likely contributed to symptom onset during running; may coexist with general asthma exacerbation.
  - Plan:
    - Review inhaler technique and adherence at GP review.
    - Consider pre-exercise SABA strategy or adjustment of maintenance therapy if EIB confirmed.
    - Advise peak flow monitoring and to bring inhalers to GP appointment.

- General plan items:
  - Bring inhalers to the face-to-face GP appointment.
  - Perform peak flow at GP visit and compare to baseline (~380 L/min reported).
  - Update asthma action plan and consider prompt review of preventer regimen if control remains poor.
  - Follow-up: face-to-face GP visit within a few days; earlier if symptoms worsen.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No objective current vital signs, respiratory exam findings, or current peak flow values recorded.
  - No formal medication doses/routes/frequencies documented for salbutamol, topical medications.
  - Smoking status and occupation not documented.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - DDx aligns with transcript for key diagnoses; only medication name discrepancy in transcript (initial mention of “Flanel Bactroban” then corrected to “Cetraben”) — conflict noted.
- Transcript quality:
  - Overall intelligible; brief unclear phrasing around topical medications required clinician clarification.
